questions.q: How many chromosomes are in a normal human somatic cell?
questions.exp: Human somatic cells are diploid with 46 chromosomes (22 autosome pairs + XX/XY).
optExp: Only autosomes counted; sex chromosomes excluded incorrectly.

questions.q: Approximately how many protein-coding genes does the human genome contain?
opts: Approximately twenty to twenty-five thousand genes
Approximately two hundred fifty thousand genes
questions.exp: Recent estimates place protein-coding genes at ~20,000-25,000 across 46 chromosomes.
optExp: That's roughly the number of SNPs in some studies, not genes.

questions.q: The centromere of a chromosome is the:
opts: Constricted region where spindle fibres attach
Repetitive sequence at the chromosome terminus
Site of gene activation during transcription
questions.exp: The centromere is the constricted region where the kinetochore assembles for spindle fibre attachment during mitosis/meiosis.

questions.q: Telomeres are:
opts: Spindle fibre attachment points at the centromere
questions.exp: Telomeres (TTAGGG repeats) cap chromosome ends, preventing end-joining and degradation. They shorten with each division.
optExp: They are DNA sequences, not modifications.

questions.q: A karyotype of 47,XXY corresponds to:
questions.exp: Klinefelter syndrome (47,XXY) — phenotypically male with hypogonadism, gynaecomastia, tall stature.

questions.q: Heterochromatin refers to:
questions.exp: Heterochromatin is densely packed and transcriptionally silent. Euchromatin is loose and active.

questions.q: The 5 histones include H2A, H2B, H3, H4 and:
questions.exp: H1 is the linker histone that binds DNA between nucleosomes, stabilising the 30-nm chromatin fibre.
optExp: H5 is avian; not standard mammalian.

questions.q: Which of the following is mitochondrially inherited?
questions.exp: LHON results from mitochondrial DNA mutations, inherited maternally from the egg's mitochondria.

questions.q: In genomic terms, an exon is a:
opts: Non-coding sequence removed during RNA processing
Coding sequence retained in mature mRNA
Promoter element located upstream of the gene
Repetitive telomeric element at chromosome end
questions.exp: Exons are retained in mature mRNA and translated. Introns are spliced out.

questions.q: What percentage of the human genome encodes proteins?
questions.exp: Only ~1-2% of the genome encodes proteins. The rest includes regulatory, structural, and non-coding RNAs.
optExp: Most of the genome is non-coding.

questions.q: A point mutation that changes a single nucleotide but does NOT alter the amino acid is called:
questions.exp: Silent mutations exploit the degeneracy of the genetic code — different codons encode the same amino acid.
optExp: Frameshift = insertion/deletion not a multiple of 3.

questions.q: A point mutation creating a premature stop codon is:
questions.exp: Nonsense mutations introduce a stop codon (UAA, UAG, UGA), truncating the protein.

questions.q: A single nucleotide insertion in a coding region is most likely to cause:
opts: Silent mutation with no phenotypic effect
Frameshift mutation disrupting the reading frame
Synonymous mutation preserving the amino acid
Conservative substitution of a similar amino acid
questions.exp: Inserting one base shifts the reading frame downstream, drastically altering the protein.
optExp: Insertions of one base are not silent.

questions.q: Sickle cell anaemia results from which mutation?
opts: Single missense mutation in the β-globin gene
Frameshift mutation in the α-globin gene
questions.exp: A single missense substitution (Glu6Val) in β-globin produces HbS, which polymerises under low O₂, sickling RBCs.
optExp: α-globin is unaffected; β-globin is altered.

questions.q: Trinucleotide repeat expansion is the mechanism of:
questions.exp: Huntington disease is caused by CAG repeat expansion in the HTT gene, with anticipation in subsequent generations.
optExp: CF is a deletion (ΔF508 most common).

questions.q: Genetic anticipation describes:
opts: Disease occurring earlier and with greater severity in successive generations
questions.exp: Trinucleotide repeat disorders (e.g. myotonic dystrophy, Huntington) typically show anticipation due to repeat expansion in gametes.
optExp: Sex-limited is different (e.g. premature ovarian failure).

questions.q: Cystic fibrosis is caused by mutations in:
questions.exp: CFTR mutations (most commonly ΔF508) disrupt chloride transport, causing thick mucus in lungs, pancreas, gut.

questions.q: Translocation refers to:
questions.exp: Translocation occurs when a chromosomal segment breaks off and reattaches to a different chromosome (e.g. BCR-ABL in CML).

questions.q: Which type of mutation results in the production of a polypeptide of altered length most directly?
questions.exp: Nonsense (premature stop) and frameshift mutations alter the polypeptide length most directly.

questions.q: Loss-of-function mutations are typically:
questions.exp: Loss of function usually requires both copies to be defective — recessive inheritance. Gain of function is typically dominant.

questions.q: Which is an autosomal DOMINANT condition?
questions.exp: Huntington disease is autosomal dominant — one mutant copy of HTT (with expanded CAG repeats) causes disease.

questions.q: Which is an X-linked recessive condition?
questions.exp: DMD is X-linked recessive — males (XY) with one mutant dystrophin allele are affected.

questions.q: Which pattern of inheritance never shows male-to-male transmission?
questions.exp: X-linked traits cannot pass father-to-son because fathers give the Y, not X, to sons. Mitochondrial is also non-male transmitted.
optExp: Mitochondrial is exclusively maternal — also fits, but X-linked is the classic answer.

questions.q: Two heterozygous carriers of an autosomal recessive disease have what risk per child of an affected offspring?
questions.exp: Aa × Aa cross: 25% AA (unaffected), 50% Aa (carrier), 25% aa (affected).
optExp: This is the probability if neither carry.
33% would be if focusing only on non-AA.
100% would only be if both are affected.

questions.q: An affected father with an autosomal dominant condition has what chance of an affected child (heterozygote × normal)?
questions.exp: Aa × aa = 50% Aa (affected), 50% aa (normal).
optExp: 25% is the autosomal recessive carrier × carrier ratio.
100% would be Aa × Aa with full penetrance + lethality of aa.

questions.q: Mitochondrial inheritance is characterised by:
questions.exp: Mitochondrial DNA comes from the egg, so mothers pass mitochondrial diseases to all children; affected fathers do not transmit.
optExp: Generally does not skip; depends on heteroplasmy.

questions.q: Penetrance refers to:
opts: Severity of phenotype in affected individuals
Proportion of genotype carriers showing the phenotype
Whether the trait is dominant or recessive
questions.exp: Penetrance = % of individuals with a disease-causing genotype who actually express it. Expressivity = how SEVERELY they express.

questions.q: Uniparental disomy gives rise to which of the following?
questions.exp: Both copies of chromosome 15 from one parent: paternal duplication → Prader-Willi; maternal → Angelman (due to imprinting).
optExp: Triploidy is dispermy or diploid gamete.

questions.q: Genomic imprinting means:
opts: Expression of only the paternal or maternal allele
Gene sequence changing with each generation
questions.exp: Imprinted genes are expressed monoallelically depending on parental origin (DNA methylation 'remembers' which parent).
optExp: Imprinting is not about new mutations.

questions.q: Heterozygote advantage explains why which disease persists in some populations?
opts: Sickle cell disease in malaria-endemic regions
questions.exp: Some recessive diseases (e.g. sickle cell vs malaria, possibly CF vs cholera/TB) persist because heterozygotes have a survival advantage.

questions.q: In which phase of mitosis do chromosomes align at the metaphase plate?
questions.exp: During metaphase, chromosomes line up in the middle of the cell with sister chromatids attached to spindle fibres.

questions.q: Sister chromatids separate to opposite poles in:
questions.exp: Anaphase: centromeres split, sister chromatids are pulled apart by shortening spindle fibres.

questions.q: DNA replication occurs during:
questions.exp: S (synthesis) phase of interphase is when DNA is replicated.

questions.q: Which checkpoint protein halts the cell cycle at G1 in response to DNA damage?
questions.exp: p53 ('guardian of the genome') arrests the cell at G1 to allow repair, or triggers apoptosis if damage is irreparable.
optExp: BRCA1 is involved in DNA repair, not checkpoint per se.
Rb regulates G1/S but is downstream.

questions.q: Meiosis produces:
questions.exp: Meiosis I + II yield 4 haploid gametes, with genetic diversity from crossing over and independent assortment.
optExp: Two haploid is only after meiosis I.
Diploid would not be a gamete.

questions.q: Crossing over occurs during which phase of meiosis?
questions.exp: Crossing over (recombination) occurs in prophase I (pachytene), generating genetic variation between homologous chromosomes.
optExp: No homologue pairing in meiosis II.

questions.q: Independent assortment of homologous chromosomes occurs in:
questions.exp: Independent assortment of HOMOLOGOUS chromosomes happens in meiosis I anaphase, contributing to genetic diversity.
optExp: Anaphase II separates SISTERS not homologues.
Mitotic anaphase doesn't involve homologue separation in this way.

questions.q: Nondisjunction in meiosis is the failure of:
questions.exp: Nondisjunction = failure of homologues (meiosis I) or sister chromatids (meiosis II) to separate, leading to aneuploidy (e.g. trisomy 21).
optExp: Cytokinesis is cell separation, not chromosome separation.

questions.q: If p53 is mutated/non-functional, the result is:
questions.exp: Without functional p53, damaged DNA isn't repaired or eliminated — cells with mutations replicate and may become cancerous.

questions.q: At the end of meiosis I, the daughter cells are:
opts: Diploid with sister chromatids still joined
Haploid with sister chromatids still joined
Genetically identical to the parent cell
questions.exp: After meiosis I, each cell is haploid (n) but each chromosome still has 2 sister chromatids. Meiosis II separates these.
optExp: No longer diploid after meiosis I.

questions.q: Epigenetic mechanisms affect gene expression without altering:
questions.exp: Epigenetic changes (methylation, histone modifications) modify gene activity without changing the DNA sequence itself.
optExp: Folding is downstream and not the definition.

questions.q: DNA methylation typically occurs at:
questions.exp: In mammals, cytosines in CpG dinucleotides are the predominant target of DNA methylation, silencing genes.
optExp: Telomeres have their own structure but methylation is CpG-targeted.

questions.q: X-inactivation in females is mediated by:
questions.exp: XIST RNA coats one X chromosome and recruits silencing machinery, forming a Barr body in females.

questions.q: Histone acetylation tends to:
opts: Activating gene expression by loosening chromatin structure
questions.exp: Acetylation neutralises positive lysine charges on histone tails, loosening DNA wrapping → euchromatin → active transcription.

questions.q: Imprinting disorders such as Prader-Willi and Angelman syndromes both involve chromosome:
questions.exp: Both result from deletion or uniparental disomy of chromosome 15q11-13 — paternal loss → Prader-Willi; maternal loss → Angelman.
optExp: CFTR is on 7 but not for these.

questions.q: Sex chromosomes in a normal human male are:
questions.exp: Normal male karyotype is 46,XY. XX is female; XO is Turner; XXY is Klinefelter; XYY is Jacobs.

questions.q: In Duchenne muscular dystrophy, the affected gene encodes:
questions.exp: DMD is caused by dystrophin gene mutations (X-linked recessive), leading to fragile muscle membranes.
optExp: Actin defects cause myopathies but not DMD.

questions.q: Myotonic dystrophy is caused by:
opts: CTG repeat expansion in DMPK gene
CAG repeat expansion in HTT gene
questions.exp: Myotonic dystrophy (autosomal dominant) results from CTG repeat expansion in DMPK, with genetic anticipation.

questions.q: Angelman syndrome results from:
opts: Paternal 15q11-q13 deletion or maternal uniparental disomy
Maternal 15q11-q13 deletion or paternal uniparental disomy
questions.exp: Angelman = loss of the maternal contribution of 15q11-13 (deletion or paternal UPD), causing severe intellectual disability and 'happy puppet' features.

questions.q: Prader-Willi syndrome results from:
opts: Paternal 15q11-q13 deletion or maternal uniparental disomy
Maternal 15q11-q13 deletion or paternal uniparental disomy
questions.exp: Prader-Willi = loss of paternal contribution to 15q11-13 → obesity, short stature, hypotonia.

questions.q: At the G2 checkpoint, the cell ensures:
opts: DNA replication is complete before mitosis
Cell reaches adequate size for division
questions.exp: G2/M checkpoint verifies DNA was replicated correctly and undamaged before allowing mitosis.
optExp: Size check is more in G1.
Spindle checkpoint is at metaphase-anaphase transition.

questions.q: A Barr body is:
questions.exp: The Barr body is the inactivated X chromosome (via XIST), visible as a dense structure in female somatic cells.

questions.q: A child with short stature, single palmar crease, hypotonia, and flat midface most likely has:
questions.exp: Trisomy 21 (Down syndrome): flat midface, single palmar crease (simian crease), hypotonia, short stature, characteristic upward palpebral slant.
optExp: Edwards: clenched fists, rocker bottom feet.

questions.q: A male infant has clenched fists with overlapping fingers, rocker-bottom feet, micrognathia, and severe heart defects. Likely diagnosis:
questions.exp: Trisomy 18 (Edwards): clenched fists, rocker-bottom feet, low-set ears, severe cardiac defects, poor survival (<1 year).
optExp: Turner is monosomy X, female phenotype.

questions.q: In a nucleosome, DNA wraps around:
questions.exp: ~147 bp of DNA wraps around a histone octamer (2 each of H2A, H2B, H3, H4) to form a nucleosome.
optExp: DNA is paired with histones, not RNA.
Backbone is part of DNA structure.

questions.q: In a pedigree, an autosomal dominant condition typically shows:
questions.exp: Autosomal dominant patterns show vertical transmission (every generation), both sexes affected equally.
optExp: Recessive may appear to skip generations.

questions.q: Sickle cell carriers (heterozygotes) have a survival advantage against:
questions.exp: Sickled red cells are inhospitable to P. falciparum, giving heterozygotes a survival advantage in malarial regions — explaining persistence of the allele.

questions.q: After S phase but before mitosis, each chromosome consists of:
opts: Two sister chromatids joined at centromere
questions.exp: DNA replication in S phase doubles each chromosome to two sister chromatids joined at the centromere, separated in mitotic anaphase.
